title: Ἀχιλλέως ἄχος
about: Antilochus runs to Achilles with the news that Patroclus is dead and that Hector has his armour. Achilles has just been fearing as much, watching the Achaeans driven back to the ships. He pours dust on his head and lies stretched out in the ashes, and the captive women wail while Antilochus holds his hands in case he cuts his own throat. His cry reaches his mother Thetis in the sea, and she rises with all the Nereids, who are named one by one, to come to him on the Trojan shore. She asks what troubles him and reminds him that Zeus has done what he wished. He answers that this means nothing now that his friend is lost, and that he will not live on unless he kills Hector. Thetis tells him that his own death will follow close behind Hector’s.

sentences.t:
ὣς οἳ μὲν μάρναντο δέμας πυρὸς αἰθομένοιο,
Ἀντίλοχος δ’ Ἀχιλῆϊ πόδας ταχὺς ἄγγελος ἦλθε.
sentences.l:
So they, for their part, fought in the likeness of blazing fire,
and Antilochus, swift in feet, came to Achilles as a messenger.
sentences.i: So they fought, like a blazing fire, while Antilochus, swift of foot, came to Achilles as a messenger.
sentences.n: Book 18 opens by turning from the fighting over Patroclus’ body to the man who must be told of it. ὣς οἳ μὲν … Ἀντίλοχος δέ sets the two scenes side by side. δέμας is an accusative of respect, ‘in body’, so δέμας πυρός is ‘in the likeness of fire’; πόδας ταχύς, ‘swift in feet’, is another such accusative. Antilochus is Nestor’s son, sent by Menelaus at the end of Book 17.

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ εὗρε προπάροιθε νεῶν ὀρθοκραιράων
τὰ φρονέοντ’ ἀνὰ θυμὸν ἃ δὴ τετελεσμένα ἦεν·
sentences.l:
Him he found in front of the straight-horned ships,
thinking over in his heart those things which indeed had been fulfilled;
sentences.i: He found him in front of the straight-horned ships, going over in his heart what had by now been fulfilled;
sentences.n: ὀρθοκραιράων ‘straight-horned’ is the word used elsewhere of cattle, here applied to ships; what the ‘horns’ of a ship are (upright prow- or stern-posts, perhaps) is not known, so only the literal sense is given. τετελεσμένα ἦεν is a pluperfect, ‘had been fulfilled’, and ἦεν is ἦν. The things fulfilled are the Achaean defeat that Achilles had wished on them, and he is brooding on it before any news has reached him.

sentences.t: ὀχθήσας δ’ ἄρα εἶπε πρὸς ὃν μεγαλήτορα θυμόν·
sentences.l: And, vexed, he then spoke to his own great-spirited heart:
sentences.i: And, troubled, he spoke to his own great-spirited heart:
sentences.n: A whole-line formula for a speech made to oneself, as at 11.403 and 17.90, and the English is the one the poem already has for it. ὀχθήσας ‘troubled’ is the aorist participle of ὀχθέω; μεγαλήτορα ‘great-spirited’ fills out ὃν θυμόν ‘his own heart’. What follows is Achilles thinking aloud, with no listener.

sentences.t:
ὤ μοι ἐγώ, τί τ’ ἄρ’ αὖτε κάρη κομόωντες Ἀχαιοὶ
νηυσὶν ἔπι κλονέονται ἀτυζόμενοι πεδίοιο;
sentences.l:
“Oh me, why then again are the long-haired-of-head Achaeans
thrown into confusion by the ships, dazed with fear, away from the plain?
sentences.i: “Oh me, why are the long-haired Achaeans again being thrown into confusion by the ships, dazed with fear, away from the plain?
sentences.n: τί τ’ ἄρ’ is ‘why, then’, and αὖτε ‘again’ recalls an earlier rout. κάρη κομόωντες, literally ‘wearing the hair long as to the head’, is the Achaeans’ stock epithet, translated every time. κλονέονται is the passive of κλονέω ‘throw into confusion’, and ἀτυζόμενοι is ‘dazed with fear’. The genitive πεδίοιο is taken as ‘away from the plain’; some read it as ‘over the plain’. He has seen the rout and fears what it means.

sentences.t: μὴ δή μοι τελέσωσι θεοὶ κακὰ κήδεα θυμῷ,
sentences.l: lest now the gods fulfil for me evil sorrows in my heart,
sentences.i: I fear the gods may now fulfil evil sorrows in my heart,
sentences.n: μή with the subjunctive τελέσωσι, after a fear that the Greek does not state, is ‘lest’; the English supplies ‘I fear’. κακὰ κήδεα is ‘evil sorrows’, and θυμῷ is a dative of place, ‘in my heart’, with μοι the dative of interest, ‘for me’. τελέσωσι ‘fulfil’ belongs to the same family as τετελεσμένα (line 4), which the speech now picks up.

sentences.t:
ὥς ποτέ μοι μήτηρ διεπέφραδε καί μοι ἔειπε
Μυρμιδόνων τὸν ἄριστον ἔτι ζώοντος ἐμεῖο
χερσὶν ὕπο Τρώων λείψειν φάος ἠελίοιο.
sentences.l:
as once my mother made plain to me and told me
that the best of the Myrmidons, while I was still living,
under the hands of the Trojans would leave the light of the sun.
sentences.i: as my mother once made plain to me and told me: that the best of the Myrmidons, while I was still alive, would leave the light of the sun beneath the hands of the Trojans.
sentences.n: ὥς is ‘just as’. διεπέφραδε is a reduplicated aorist of διαφράζω ‘point out, make plain’. τὸν ἄριστον ‘the best one’ is the subject of the infinitive λείψειν ‘would leave’, and ἔτι ζώοντος ἐμεῖο is a genitive absolute, ‘with me still alive’; ἐμεῖο is the epic genitive of ἐγώ. ‘To leave the light of the sun’ is to die. The warning is Thetis’ own, so Achilles is recalling her words.

sentences.t:
ἦ μάλα δὴ τέθνηκε Μενοιτίου ἄλκιμος υἱὸς
σχέτλιος·
sentences.l:
Truly, very much so, he is dead, Menoetius’ sturdy son,
cruel one;
sentences.i: Surely Menoetius’ sturdy son is dead by now, the cruel one;
sentences.n: ἦ μάλα δὴ is a strong ‘surely’. τέθνηκε, perfect, has a present sense: ‘he is dead’. Μενοιτίου ἄλκιμος υἱός is Patroclus’ stock phrase, and he is not named until Antilochus names him. σχέτλιος is the house ‘cruel one’; the word has a range (hard, unyielding, headstrong), and here it is half reproach and half grief at a man who would not turn back.

sentences.t:
ἦ τ’ ἐκέλευον ἀπωσάμενον δήϊον πῦρ
ἂψ ἐπὶ νῆας ἴμεν, μηδ’ Ἕκτορι ἶφι μάχεσθαι.
sentences.l:
truly I was ordering him, once he had thrust away the hostile fire,
back to the ships to go, and not with Hector to fight with force.”
sentences.i: I did tell him, once he had thrust away the hostile fire, to go back to the ships and not to fight Hector powerfully.”
sentences.n: ἦ τε is ‘truly’. ἐκέλευον is imperfect, ‘I was ordering’ (‘bid’ is kept for ἄνωγα). ἀπωσάμενον is an aorist middle participle of ἀπωθέω, agreeing with the unexpressed ‘him’, and δήϊον πῦρ is ‘hostile fire’. ἴμεν is the epic infinitive of εἶμι ‘go’. ἶφι, ‘with force’, is given as ‘powerfully’, as at 1.151. Achilles’ order to Patroclus is recalled here and it is the moment that his fear becomes a judgement.

sentences.t:
εἷος ὃ ταῦθ’ ὥρμαινε κατὰ φρένα καὶ κατὰ θυμόν,
τόφρά οἱ ἐγγύθεν ἦλθεν ἀγαυοῦ Νέστορος υἱὸς
δάκρυα θερμὰ χέων, φάτο δ’ ἀγγελίην ἀλεγεινήν·
sentences.l:
While he was pondering these things in mind and in heart,
meanwhile came near to him the son of noble Nestor,
tears hot shedding, and he spoke grievous news:
sentences.i: While he was turning this over in his mind and heart, the son of noble Nestor came up close to him, shedding hot tears, and he told his grievous news:
sentences.n: εἷος ‘while’ and τόφρα ‘meanwhile’ answer each other. ὥρμαινε is the imperfect of ὁρμαίνω ‘ponder, turn over’. κατὰ φρένα καὶ κατὰ θυμόν is ‘in mind and in heart’, a pair the poem often uses. ‘The son of noble Nestor’ is Antilochus, already named at line 2; ἀγαυοῦ is ‘noble’, and ἐγγύθεν is ‘from near by’. δάκρυα θερμὰ χέων is ‘shedding hot tears’. φάτο is the aorist middle of φημί, ‘he said’, here with the news as its object. ἀγγελίην ἀλεγεινήν is ‘grievous news’, the pairing used elsewhere in the poem; the speech uses λυγρῆς for the same idea.

sentences.t:
ὤ μοι Πηλέος υἱὲ δαΐφρονος ἦ μάλα λυγρῆς
πεύσεαι ἀγγελίης, ἣ μὴ ὤφελλε γενέσθαι.
sentences.l:
“Oh me, son of wise-minded Peleus, truly very grievous
news you will learn, which, would that it had not come to be.
sentences.i: “Oh me, son of wise-hearted Peleus, you will learn truly grievous news — if only it had not happened.
sentences.n: ὤ μοι is ‘oh me’, Πηλέος the epic genitive of Πηλεύς, and δαΐφρων is ‘wise-hearted’, though ‘wise’ or ‘fierce’ is not settled. πεύσεαι is the future of πυνθάνομαι ‘learn, find out’. ὤφελλε with the infinitive is a wish that cannot now be met: ‘would that it had not come to be’. Antilochus speaks of the news before he can say it.

sentences.t:
κεῖται Πάτροκλος, νέκυος δὲ δὴ ἀμφιμάχονται
γυμνοῦ· ἀτὰρ τά γε τεύχε’ ἔχει κορυθαίολος Ἕκτωρ.
sentences.l:
Patroclus lies low, and around his corpse they are fighting,
naked; but that armour Hector of the glancing helmet has.”
sentences.i: Patroclus lies dead, and they are fighting around his corpse, naked as it is; but Hector of the glancing helmet has the armour.”
sentences.n: κεῖται ‘lies’ means ‘lies dead’. νέκυος … γυμνοῦ is the genitive after ἀμφιμάχονται, ‘fight around’; ‘naked’ means stripped of his armour, which the next clause says Hector holds. ἀτάρ is ‘but’, and κορυθαίολος is ‘of the glancing helmet’, the house rendering. The speech ends with the worst fact placed last.

sentences.t: ὣς φάτο, τὸν δ’ ἄχεος νεφέλη ἐκάλυψε μέλαινα·
sentences.l: So he spoke, and him a cloud of grief covered, dark;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and a dark cloud of grief covered Achilles;
sentences.n: ‘He’ is Antilochus. The line is the one that fell on Hector at 17.591, and it is a standard image for a blow that blinds the mind: ἄχεος νεφέλη, ‘a cloud of grief’, with μέλαινα ‘dark’ placed last. The Greek has only τόν ‘him’; the English names Achilles to keep the speaker and the listener apart.

sentences.t:
ἀμφοτέρῃσι δὲ χερσὶν ἑλὼν κόνιν αἰθαλόεσσαν
χεύατο κὰκ κεφαλῆς, χαρίεν δ’ ᾔσχυνε πρόσωπον·
sentences.l:
and with both hands taking sooty dust
he poured it down from over his head, and disfigured his graceful face;
sentences.i: and taking sooty dust in both hands he poured it down over his head and disfigured his graceful face;
sentences.n: Throwing dust on the head is the gesture of mourning. κόνιν αἰθαλόεσσαν is ‘sooty dust’ (ash), with the epic double σ. κὰκ κεφαλῆς is κατὰ κεφαλῆς with the κ assimilated: ‘down from the head’. ᾔσχυνε, from αἰσχύνω, is ‘disfigured’, and χαρίεν ‘graceful’ agrees with πρόσωπον ‘face’.

sentences.t: νεκταρέῳ δὲ χιτῶνι μέλαιν’ ἀμφίζανε τέφρη.
sentences.l: and on his nectar-sweet tunic black ash settled all about.
sentences.i: and black ash settled all over his tunic, sweet as nectar.
sentences.n: νεκταρέῳ is ‘nectar-sweet’, read as ‘like nectar’ (the usual explanation); what exactly is meant of a tunic, whether scent or fineness, is not known. ἀμφίζανε is an imperfect, ‘settled round’, and τέφρη is ‘ash’. The ash falls on the fine tunic, so the picture is of dirt on what was clean.

sentences.t:
αὐτὸς δ’ ἐν κονίῃσι μέγας μεγαλωστὶ τανυσθεὶς
κεῖτο, φίλῃσι δὲ χερσὶ κόμην ᾔσχυνε δαΐζων.
sentences.l:
And he himself in the dust, great in his greatness, stretched out,
lay, and with his own hands his hair he disfigured, tearing it.
sentences.i: He himself lay stretched out at full length in the dust, and with his own hands he disfigured his hair, tearing at it.
sentences.n: αὐτός ‘he himself’ sets Achilles against the maidservants who come next. μέγας μεγαλωστί, ‘great in his greatness’, is given as ‘at full length’, as it is for the dead man at 16.776; τανυσθείς is ‘stretched out’. κονίῃσι is the epic dative plural of κονία ‘dust’. φίλῃσι χερσί is ‘with his own hands’, and δαΐζων ‘tearing’ is the participle of δαΐζω, with ᾔσχυνε repeated from line 24.

sentences.t:
δμῳαὶ δ’ ἃς Ἀχιλεὺς ληΐσσατο Πάτροκλός τε
θυμὸν ἀκηχέμεναι μεγάλ’ ἴαχον, ἐκ δὲ θύραζε
ἔδραμον ἀμφ’ Ἀχιλῆα δαΐφρονα,
sentences.l:
And the maidservants whom Achilles took as spoil, and Patroclus,
sorrowing at heart, cried out loudly, and out of doors
ran about Achilles, wise-minded,
sentences.i: The maidservants whom Achilles and Patroclus had taken as spoil, grieved at heart, cried out loudly and ran out of doors around wise-hearted Achilles,
sentences.n: These are captives taken in raids, and ἃς Ἀχιλεὺς ληΐσσατο Πάτροκλός τε says that both men took them. ἀκηχέμεναι is a perfect participle, ‘sorrowing’, with θυμόν as an accusative of respect, ‘at heart’. ἴαχον is ‘cried out loudly’, and θύραζε ‘out of doors’. δαΐφρων is ‘wise-hearted’, though whether it means ‘wise’ or ‘fierce’ is not settled.

sentences.t:
χερσὶ δὲ πᾶσαι
στήθεα πεπλήγοντο, λύθεν δ’ ὑπὸ γυῖα ἑκάστης.
sentences.l:
and with their hands all
beat their breasts, and loosed beneath were the limbs of each.
sentences.i: and all of them beat their breasts with their hands, and the limbs of each gave way beneath her.
sentences.n: πεπλήγοντο is a reduplicated aorist middle of πλήσσω: they struck their own breasts, the gesture of women’s lament. λύθεν is the aorist passive of λύω, ‘were loosed’; the limbs, the knees especially, go slack with grief, a figure the poem also uses of death. Here nobody is killed.

sentences.t:
Ἀντίλοχος δ’ ἑτέρωθεν ὀδύρετο δάκρυα λείβων
χεῖρας ἔχων Ἀχιλῆος·
sentences.l:
And Antilochus on the other side lamented, tears pouring,
holding the hands of Achilles;
sentences.i: Antilochus on the other side lamented, pouring out his tears, and held Achilles’ hands;
sentences.n: ἑτέρωθεν is ‘from the other side’, opposite the women. ὀδύρετο, ‘lamented’, takes δάκρυα λείβων, ‘pouring out his tears’. Why he holds Achilles’ hands is given two lines later.

sentences.t: ὃ δ’ ἔστενε κυδάλιμον κῆρ·
sentences.l: and he groaned in his glorious heart;
sentences.i: and Achilles groaned in his glorious heart;
sentences.n: ὃ δέ ‘and he’ turns back to Achilles, and the English names him. ἔστενε is an imperfect, ‘was groaning’. κυδάλιμον κῆρ, ‘glorious heart’, is an accusative of respect, ‘in his heart’.

sentences.t: δείδιε γὰρ μὴ λαιμὸν ἀπαμήσειε σιδήρῳ.
sentences.l: for he feared lest he cut his throat with iron.
sentences.i: for Antilochus feared that Achilles would cut his own throat with the iron.
sentences.n: δείδιε is a perfect with present sense, here used of past time. μή with the optative ἀπαμήσειε is ‘lest he cut through’, from ἀπαμάω. The Greek does not name either man: the one afraid is Antilochus and the one who might cut is Achilles, and the English says so. σίδηρος ‘iron’ stands for a blade, as it stood for the arrowhead at 4.123.

sentences.t: σμερδαλέον δ’ ᾤμωξεν·
sentences.l: And terribly he wailed;
sentences.i: And he cried out terribly;
sentences.n: σμερδαλέον is a neuter adjective used as an adverb, ‘terribly’. ᾤμωξεν, ‘wailed’ in the literal English and ‘cried out’ in the free, is from οἰμώζω. The subject is Achilles, and the cry is what sends the news under the sea.

sentences.t:
ἄκουσε δὲ πότνια μήτηρ
ἡμένη ἐν βένθεσσιν ἁλὸς παρὰ πατρὶ γέροντι,
κώκυσέν τ’ ἄρ’ ἔπειτα·
sentences.i: and his lady mother heard him, as she sat in the depths of the sea beside her old father, and then she cried out;
sentences.n: ἄκουσε has no object in the Greek, and ‘him’ is understood; at 1.357 the same mother’s hearing has τοῦ ‘him’ expressed. ἡμένη ‘sitting’ and βένθεσσιν, the epic dative plural of βένθος ‘depth’, give her place. The old father is Nereus, whom the poem does not name here. κώκυσε is the shrill cry of lament, and τ’ ἄρ’ ἔπειτα is ‘and then’.

sentences.t:
θεαὶ δέ μιν ἀμφαγέροντο
πᾶσαι ὅσαι κατὰ βένθος ἁλὸς Νηρηΐδες ἦσαν.
sentences.l:
and the goddesses gathered around her,
all as many as in the depth of the sea were Nereids.
sentences.i: and the goddesses gathered round her, every Nereid there was in the depths of the sea.
sentences.n: The Nereids are the sea-goddesses, daughters of Nereus. ἀμφαγέροντο is an aorist of ἀμφαγείρομαι ‘gather around’, and μιν is ‘her’. πᾶσαι ὅσαι is ‘all as many as’, and the list that follows says who they are.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ ἄρ’ ἔην Γλαύκη τε Θάλειά τε Κυμοδόκη τε
Νησαίη Σπειώ τε Θόη θ’ Ἁλίη τε βοῶπις
Κυμοθόη τε καὶ Ἀκταίη καὶ Λιμνώρεια,
sentences.l:
There then were Glauce and Thaleia and Cymodoce,
Nesaea and Speio and Thoe and ox-eyed Halia,
Cymothoe and Actaea and Limnoreia,
sentences.i: There were Glauce, Thaleia and Cymodoce, Nesaea, Speio, Thoe and ox-eyed Halia, Cymothoe, Actaea and Limnoreia,
sentences.n: A catalogue of Nereids, with their names in the usual English forms. Most are sea-words that can be read: Γλαύκη ‘grey-green’, Θάλεια ‘blooming’, Κυμοδόκη ‘wave-receiver’, Νησαίη ‘of the island’, Σπειώ ‘of the cave’, Θόη ‘swift’, Ἁλίη ‘of the sea’, Κυμοθόη ‘wave-swift’, Ἀκταίη ‘of the shore’; the sense of Λιμνώρεια is not clear. Only Halia has an epithet, βοῶπις ‘ox-eyed’, the one given to Hera.

sentences.t:
καὶ Μελίτη καὶ Ἴαιρα καὶ Ἀμφιθόη καὶ Ἀγαυὴ
Δωτώ τε Πρωτώ τε Φέρουσά τε Δυναμένη τε
Δεξαμένη τε καὶ Ἀμφινόμη καὶ Καλλιάνειρα,
sentences.l:
and Melite and Iaera and Amphithoe and Agave,
Doto and Proto and Pherusa and Dynamene,
Dexamene and Amphinome and Callianeira,
sentences.i: Melite, Iaera, Amphithoe and Agave, Doto, Proto, Pherusa and Dynamene, Dexamene, Amphinome and Callianeira,
sentences.n: The catalogue goes on. Some names can be read: Μελίτη ‘honey’, Ἀμφιθόη ‘swift all round’, Ἀγαυή ‘noble’, Δωτώ ‘giver’, Πρωτώ ‘first’, Φέρουσα ‘bearer’, Δυναμένη ‘the able one’, Δεξαμένη ‘receiver’. Ἴαιρα and the second half of Καλλιάνειρα are less clear, and no meaning is claimed for them.

sentences.t:
Δωρὶς καὶ Πανόπη καὶ ἀγακλειτὴ Γαλάτεια
Νημερτής τε καὶ Ἀψευδὴς καὶ Καλλιάνασσα·
sentences.l:
Doris and Panope and renowned Galatea,
Nemertes and Apseudes and Callianassa;
sentences.i: Doris, Panope and renowned Galatea, Nemertes, Apseudes and Callianassa;
sentences.n: Πανόπη is ‘all-seeing’, Γαλάτεια ‘milk-white’, Νημερτής ‘unerring’ and Ἀψευδής ‘truthful’, and Καλλιάνασσα ‘fair queen’; Δωρίς may be ‘gift’. ἀγακλειτή ‘renowned’ is the epithet on Galatea, the only one in this run. The high stop (·) marks the pause before the last group.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα δ’ ἔην Κλυμένη Ἰάνειρά τε καὶ Ἰάνασσα
Μαῖρα καὶ Ὠρείθυια ἐϋπλόκαμός τ’ Ἀμάθεια
ἄλλαι θ’ αἳ κατὰ βένθος ἁλὸς Νηρηΐδες ἦσαν.
sentences.l:
and there were Clymene and Ianeira and Ianassa,
Maera and Oreithyia and fine-plaited Amatheia,
and other Nereids who were in the depth of the sea.
sentences.i: and there were Clymene, Ianeira and Ianassa, Maera, Oreithyia and fine-plaited Amatheia, and the other Nereids who were in the depths of the sea.
sentences.n: The last names: Κλυμένη ‘famous’; Ἰάνειρα and Ἰάνασσα are not clear, and neither is Μαῖρα. ἐϋπλόκαμος ‘fine-plaited’ is the house rendering. Line 49 nearly repeats line 38, closing the list as it opened.

sentences.t: τῶν δὲ καὶ ἀργύφεον πλῆτο σπέος·
sentences.l: and of them the silver-white cave was filled;
sentences.i: and the silver-white cave was filled with them;
sentences.n: τῶν is a genitive after πλῆτο, ‘was filled with them’, the epic aorist of πίμπλημι. ἀργύφεον is ‘silver-white’. σπέος is the cave under the sea where Thetis lives with her father.

sentences.t:
αἳ δ’ ἅμα πᾶσαι
στήθεα πεπλήγοντο, Θέτις δ’ ἐξῆρχε γόοιο·
sentences.l:
and they all together
beat their breasts, and Thetis led off the lament:
sentences.i: and all of them together beat their breasts, and Thetis led off the lament:
sentences.n: The Nereids beat their breasts as the maidservants did at lines 30–31. ἐξῆρχε with the genitive γόοιο ‘lament’ means to begin it; in a group lament one voice starts, and the others take it up. The colon introduces Thetis’ words.

sentences.t:
κλῦτε κασίγνηται Νηρηΐδες, ὄφρ’ ἐῢ πᾶσαι
εἴδετ’ ἀκούουσαι ὅσ’ ἐμῷ ἔνι κήδεα θυμῷ.
sentences.l:
“Hear, sister Nereids, so that well all of you
may know, hearing, how many sorrows are in my heart.
sentences.i: “Hear me, sister Nereids, so that you may all know well, as you listen, how many sorrows are in my heart.
sentences.n: κλῦτε is an imperative, ‘hear’. κασίγνηται Νηρηΐδες is a vocative pair, ‘sisters, Nereids’. ὄφρα with εἴδετ’ (= εἰδῆτε, subjunctive of οἶδα) is ‘so that you may know’. ἐμῷ ἔνι … θυμῷ is ‘in my heart’ (ἔνι is ἐνί read as the preposition; some take it as ἔνεστι, ‘is in’), so ὅσ’ … κήδεα is ‘how many sorrows’.

sentences.t: ὤ μοι ἐγὼ δειλή, ὤ μοι δυσαριστοτόκεια,
sentences.l: Oh me, miserable that I am, oh me, ill-fated mother of the best,
sentences.i: Oh me, miserable that I am, unhappy mother of the best,
sentences.n: δειλή is ‘miserable’. δυσαριστοτόκεια occurs only here; it is built from δυσ- ‘ill’, ἄριστος ‘best’ and τόκος ‘bearing’, so the sense is ‘who bore the best, to her sorrow’, read from the parts. The second ὤ μοι answers the first.

sentences.t:
ἥ τ’ ἐπεὶ ἂρ τέκον υἱὸν ἀμύμονά τε κρατερόν τε
ἔξοχον ἡρώων·
sentences.l:
who, when I bore a son both blameless and strong,
standing out above the heroes,
sentences.i: who bore a son, blameless and strong, standing out above the heroes;
sentences.n: ἥ τε ‘I who’ goes back to ἐγώ in line 54. ἐπεὶ ἂρ τέκον is ‘when I bore’, and ἂρ is ἄρα. ἀμύμονα is ‘blameless’, the house rendering of a word whose real sense is not known, and κρατερόν is ‘strong’. ἔξοχον ἡρώων, ‘standing out above the heroes’, takes the genitive of comparison. The relative clause has no main verb of its own, and the story simply goes on at line 56.

sentences.t: ὃ δ’ ἀνέδραμεν ἔρνεϊ ἶσος·
sentences.l: and he ran up equal to a sapling;
sentences.i: and he sprang up like a young sapling;
sentences.n: ἀνέδραμεν, the aorist of ἀνατρέχω, is ‘ran up’, said of fast growth. ἔρνεϊ ἶσος is ‘equal to a sapling’, the house phrase, with the dative after ἶσος. The plant image carries into the next line.

sentences.t:
τὸν μὲν ἐγὼ θρέψασα φυτὸν ὣς γουνῷ ἀλωῆς
νηυσὶν ἐπιπροέηκα κορωνίσιν Ἴλιον εἴσω
Τρωσὶ μαχησόμενον·
sentences.i: I reared him like a plant on the rich ground of an orchard, and sent him forth in the curved ships to Ilium to fight the Trojans;
sentences.n: θρέψασα ‘having reared’ with φυτὸν ὣς … is ‘like a plant’; γουνῷ ἀλωῆς is ‘on the rich ground of the orchard’, as at 9.534, and the sense of γουνός is not certain. ἐπιπροέηκα is the aorist of ἐπιπροΐημι ‘send forth upon’. κορωνίσιν is the house ‘curved’. μαχησόμενον is a future participle of purpose, ‘to fight’. τὸν μέν looks ahead to τὸν δέ in the next unit.

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ οὐχ ὑποδέξομαι αὖτις
οἴκαδε νοστήσαντα δόμον Πηλήϊον εἴσω.
sentences.l:
but him I shall not receive again
returned home into the house of Peleus.
sentences.i: but I shall not receive him back again, returned home into the house of Peleus.
sentences.n: τὸν δ’ is the answering ‘but him’. ὑποδέξομαι, a future, is ‘I shall receive’. νοστήσαντα is an aorist participle, ‘having come home’, and δόμον Πηλήϊον is ‘the house of Peleus’, the adjective of Peleus, with εἴσω ‘into’. Achilles will use these words back to her at lines 89–90.

sentences.t:
ὄφρα δέ μοι ζώει καὶ ὁρᾷ φάος ἠελίοιο
ἄχνυται, οὐδέ τί οἱ δύναμαι χραισμῆσαι ἰοῦσα.
sentences.l:
But while he lives for me and sees the light of the sun,
he is grieved, and I cannot at all help him by going.
sentences.i: But while he lives and sees the light of the sun, he is grieved, and I cannot help him at all by going to him.
sentences.n: ὄφρα δέ is ‘but so long as’. μοι ζώει is ‘lives for me’, a dative of interest. ὁρᾷ φάος ἠελίοιο is ‘sees the light of the sun’, to be alive. ἄχνυται is ‘is grieved’, and χραισμῆσαι ‘to help’ takes the dative οἱ. ἰοῦσα is a participle of εἶμι, ‘by going’. She can do nothing for him while he lives, which is why she goes at once.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ εἶμ’, ὄφρα ἴδωμι φίλον τέκος, ἠδ’ ἐπακούσω
ὅττί μιν ἵκετο πένθος ἀπὸ πτολέμοιο μένοντα.
sentences.l:
But I shall go, that I may see my dear child, and hear
what grief has come to him as he stays away from the war.”
sentences.i: But I will go, to see my dear child and to hear what grief has come to him as he holds back from the war.”
sentences.n: εἶμ’ is a present with future sense, ‘I will go’. ὄφρα ἴδωμι, a subjunctive, is ‘that I may see’, and ἐπακούσω is ‘hear’. ὅττι is ὅ τι, ‘what’, an indirect question. μένοντα ‘staying’ with ἀπὸ πτολέμοιο is ‘keeping away from the war’. The speech ends with her setting out.

sentences.t: ὣς ἄρα φωνήσασα λίπε σπέος·
sentences.l: So then, having spoken, she left the cave;
sentences.i: With these words she left the cave;
sentences.n: ὣς ἄρα φωνήσασα is the formula for ‘with these words’, here for a woman. λίπε is the aorist of λείπω, ‘left’. A new paragraph begins with the journey.

sentences.t:
αἳ δὲ σὺν αὐτῇ
δακρυόεσσαι ἴσαν, περὶ δέ σφισι κῦμα θαλάσσης
ῥήγνυτο·
sentences.i: and they went with her in tears, while the wave of the sea broke about them;
sentences.n: αἳ δέ is ‘and they’, the Nereids. δακρυόεσσαι ‘tearful’ agrees with them. ἴσαν is the imperfect of εἶμι, ‘went’, and σφισι is ‘about them’, a dative. ῥήγνυτο, an imperfect middle of ῥήγνυμι ‘break’, is ‘was breaking’; the Greek does not say whether the sea opened for them.

sentences.t:
ταὶ δ’ ὅτε δὴ Τροίην ἐρίβωλον ἵκοντο
ἀκτὴν εἰσανέβαινον ἐπισχερώ,
sentences.l:
and when they came to rich-clodded Troy,
they climbed up onto the shore in a row,
sentences.i: and when they came to rich-soiled Troy, they went up onto the shore one after another,
sentences.n: ταὶ δ’ ὅτε is ‘and when they’. Τροίην ἐρίβωλον is ‘rich-soiled Troy’, the house rendering, and Τροίη is the land of Troy, not the city. ἀκτήν ‘shore’ is an accusative of goal, and εἰσανέβαινον is ‘went up onto’. ἐπισχερώ is ‘one after another’, in a line.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα θαμειαὶ
Μυρμιδόνων εἴρυντο νέες ταχὺν ἀμφ’ Ἀχιλῆα.
sentences.l:
where, thick-set,
the ships of the Myrmidons were drawn up around swift Achilles.
sentences.i: where the ships of the Myrmidons lay drawn up close together around swift Achilles.
sentences.n: θαμειαί is ‘close-set’. εἴρυντο is a pluperfect passive of ἐρύω ‘draw up’, not the middle ἐρύομαι ‘guard’, so the ships ‘had been drawn up’. Μυρμιδόνων νέες ‘ships of the Myrmidons’ are Achilles’ own; ταχύν ‘swift’ is the epithet on Ἀχιλῆα.

sentences.t: τῷ δὲ βαρὺ στενάχοντι παρίστατο πότνια μήτηρ,
sentences.l: And beside him, groaning heavily, stood his lady mother,
sentences.i: As he groaned heavily, his lady mother stood beside him,
sentences.n: τῷ … στενάχοντι is a dative participle, ‘to him groaning’, and παρίστατο is an imperfect, ‘stood beside’. βαρύ is ‘heavily’, the adverb of the formula βαρὺ στενάχων. πότνια μήτηρ ‘lady mother’ is Thetis, now at his side.

sentences.t:
ὀξὺ δὲ κωκύσασα κάρη λάβε παιδὸς ἑοῖο,
καί ῥ’ ὀλοφυρομένη ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.l:
and, having cried out shrilly, she took hold of the head of her own child,
and, lamenting, winged words she spoke:
sentences.i: and with a shrill cry she took hold of her child’s head and, lamenting, spoke winged words:
sentences.n: ὀξύ is ‘shrilly’, and κωκύσασα ‘having cried out’ is the aorist participle of κωκύω. κάρη λάβε is ‘took hold of the head’, an embrace; ἑοῖο is ‘her own’. The second line is a stock formula: ὀλοφυρομένη ‘lamenting’ and ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα ‘she spoke winged words’.

sentences.t: τέκνον τί κλαίεις;
sentences.l: “Child, why do you weep?
sentences.i: “Child, why are you weeping?
sentences.n: The same words open her question to him at 1.362, where she first came up out of the sea to him as he sat weeping. τέκνον ‘child’ is the house word, not ‘son’. κλαίεις is ‘weep’. The question that follows is asked in the next unit.

sentences.t: τί δέ σε φρένας ἵκετο πένθος;
sentences.l: And what grief has come to your wits?
sentences.i: And what grief has come over your mind?
sentences.n: As at 1.362: τί δέ σε φρένας ἵκετο πένθος has σε φρένας as a double accusative, ‘you, in your wits’, the whole and then the part. πένθος is ‘grief’, and ἵκετο ‘has come’. She asks what she has already guessed.

sentences.t: ἐξαύδα, μὴ κεῦθε·
sentences.l: Speak out, do not hide it;
sentences.i: Speak it out, do not keep it hidden;
sentences.n: ἐξαύδα is an imperative, ‘speak out’, and κεῦθε an imperative of κεύθω ‘hide’, here with μή ‘do not’. The words match 1.363, where νόῳ ‘in your mind’ completes the sense.

sentences.t:
τὰ μὲν δή τοι τετέλεσται
ἐκ Διός,
sentences.l:
those things indeed for you have been fulfilled
by Zeus,
sentences.i: Those things have indeed been fulfilled for you by Zeus,
sentences.n: τὰ μὲν δή τοι is ‘those things indeed for you’, the dative being ethic. τετέλεσται is the perfect passive of τελέω ‘fulfil’, the third use of that family (lines 4, 8, 74). ἐκ Διός, ‘from Zeus’, gives the doer. What he did is spelled out in the next unit.

sentences.t:
ὡς ἄρα δὴ πρίν γ’ εὔχεο χεῖρας ἀνασχὼν
πάντας ἐπὶ πρύμνῃσιν ἀλήμεναι υἷας Ἀχαιῶν
σεῦ ἐπιδευομένους, παθέειν τ’ ἀεκήλια ἔργα.
sentences.l:
as you prayed before, raising your hands,
that all the sons of the Achaeans at the sterns be crowded together,
lacking you, and suffer unwelcome deeds.”
sentences.i: just as you prayed before, with your hands raised, that all the sons of the Achaeans be crowded together at the sterns, lacking you, and suffer unwelcome deeds.”
sentences.n: ὡς ἄρα δὴ πρίν γ’ is ‘just as before’, and εὔχεο, an imperfect middle, is ‘you prayed’. χεῖρας ἀνασχών is ‘raising your hands’. ἀλήμεναι is an aorist passive infinitive, ‘be crowded together’, and πρύμνῃσιν ‘at the sterns’ is the beached ships’ back ends. σεῦ ἐπιδευομένους is ‘lacking you’. ἀεκήλια is a rare word, probably ‘unwelcome’ (compare ἀέκων ‘unwilling’), though the exact sense is not certain. The wish she describes is the defeat of the Achaeans.

sentences.t: τὴν δὲ βαρὺ στενάχων προσέφη πόδας ὠκὺς Ἀχιλλεύς·
sentences.l: Her, groaning heavily, addressed swift-in-feet Achilles:
sentences.i: Groaning heavily, Achilles, swift of foot, said to her:
sentences.n: A whole-line reply formula, as at 1.364, and the English is the same. τὴν δέ ‘her’ is Thetis, and βαρὺ στενάχων is ‘groaning heavily’. πόδας ὠκύς is ‘swift of foot’, the stock epithet of Achilles. Here the tone is not argument but grief.

sentences.t: μῆτερ ἐμή, τὰ μὲν ἄρ μοι Ὀλύμπιος ἐξετέλεσσεν·
sentences.l: “My mother, those things indeed the Olympian has fulfilled for me;
sentences.i: “My mother, the Olympian has fulfilled those things for me;
sentences.n: μῆτερ ἐμή is ‘my mother’. τὰ μέν picks up her ‘those things’, and ἐξετέλεσσεν, an aorist with the epic double σ, is ‘fulfilled’. Ὀλύμπιος, ‘the Olympian’, is Zeus without his name.

sentences.l:
but what pleasure is there for me in these, since my dear companion has perished,
Patroclus, whom I honoured above all companions
equally with my own head?
sentences.i: but what pleasure have I in them, now that my dear companion has perished, Patroclus, whom I honoured above all my companions, as much as my own head?
sentences.n: τί μοι τῶν ἦδος is ‘what pleasure for me of these things’, and the exact sense of ἦδος is not certain. ὤλεθ’ is the aorist of ὄλλυμι, ‘perished’. τῖον is an imperfect of τίω ‘honour’, and ἶσον ἐμῇ κεφαλῇ, ‘equally with my own head’, treats the head as the man himself: as much as my own self.

sentences.t:
τὸν ἀπώλεσα, τεύχεα δ’ Ἕκτωρ
δῃώσας ἀπέδυσε πελώρια θαῦμα ἰδέσθαι
καλά·
sentences.i: I lost him, and Hector cut him down and stripped off the armour, huge, a wonder to look at, and fine;
sentences.n: ἀπώλεσα is the aorist of ἀπόλλυμι ‘lose’. δῃώσας is an aorist participle of δηϊόω ‘cut down’, and ἀπέδυσε ‘stripped off’. τεύχεα is ‘armour’; πελώρια θαῦμα ἰδέσθαι καλά is ‘huge, a wonder to behold, fine’. The armour was Achilles’ own, worn by Patroclus, and the next unit says where it came from.

sentences.t:
τὰ μὲν Πηλῆϊ θεοὶ δόσαν ἀγλαὰ δῶρα
ἤματι τῷ ὅτε σε βροτοῦ ἀνέρος ἔμβαλον εὐνῇ.
sentences.l:
which the gods gave to Peleus, splendid gifts,
on that day when they cast you into the bed of a mortal man.
sentences.i: the gods gave them to Peleus as splendid gifts on the day they put you in the bed of a mortal man.
sentences.n: τὰ μέν goes back to the armour. δόσαν is the epic aorist ἔδοσαν without its augment, ‘gave’, and ἀγλαὰ δῶρα is ‘splendid gifts’. ἤματι τῷ ὅτε is ‘on that day when’. ἔμβαλον is ‘put into’, with εὐνῇ ‘bed’ in the dative, and βροτοῦ ἀνέρος is ‘a mortal man’. The day is the wedding of Peleus and Thetis.

sentences.t:
αἴθ’ ὄφελες σὺ μὲν αὖθι μετ’ ἀθανάτῃς ἁλίῃσι
ναίειν, Πηλεὺς δὲ θνητὴν ἀγαγέσθαι ἄκοιτιν.
sentences.l:
If only you had stayed right there among the immortal women of the sea
to dwell, and Peleus had taken a mortal wife.
sentences.i: If only you had stayed right there, living among the immortal women of the sea, and Peleus had taken a mortal wife.
sentences.n: αἴθ’ ὄφελες is ‘if only you had’, followed by the infinitive ναίειν ‘dwell’. The infinitive ἀγαγέσθαι ‘to take as his own’ is parallel, with the verb of wishing understood for Peleus. ἀθανάτῃς is an epic form for the dative plural, and ἁλίῃσι is ‘of the sea’ used as a noun, the sea-goddesses. ἄκοιτιν is ‘wife’.

sentences.t:
νῦν δ’ ἵνα καὶ σοὶ πένθος ἐνὶ φρεσὶ μυρίον εἴη
παιδὸς ἀποφθιμένοιο,
sentences.l:
But now, so that for you too there may be countless grief in your wits
for a child having perished,
sentences.i: But now, so that you too may have countless grief in your mind for a son who has perished,
sentences.n: νῦν δ’ is ‘but as it is’. ἵνα with the optative εἴη is ‘so that … may be’, said bitterly, as if the gods had planned it. μυρίον is ‘countless’. ἀποφθιμένοιο is an aorist middle participle, ‘having perished’; he is still alive, and Achilles speaks of his death as settled.

sentences.t:
τὸν οὐχ ὑποδέξεαι αὖτις
οἴκαδε νοστήσαντ’,
sentences.l:
whom you will not receive again
returned home,
sentences.i: whom you will not receive back again, returned home,
sentences.n: ὑποδέξεαι, a second-person future, is ‘you will receive’. These are Thetis’ own words at lines 59–60, handed back to her, and the English matches. νοστήσαντ’ is an aorist participle with the final vowel elided.

sentences.t:
ἐπεὶ οὐδ’ ἐμὲ θυμὸς ἄνωγε
ζώειν οὐδ’ ἄνδρεσσι μετέμμεναι,
sentences.l:
since neither does my spirit bid me
live, nor be among men,
sentences.i: since my spirit does not bid me go on living or be among men,
sentences.n: ἐπεὶ οὐδ’ … οὐδ’ is ‘since neither … nor’. ἄνωγε is a perfect with present sense, ‘bids’, and ζώειν is ‘to live’. μετέμμεναι is the epic infinitive of μέτειμι ‘to be among’. He does not want to live on unless the condition in the next unit is met.

sentences.t:
αἴ κε μὴ Ἕκτωρ
πρῶτος ἐμῷ ὑπὸ δουρὶ τυπεὶς ἀπὸ θυμὸν ὀλέσσῃ,
sentences.l:
unless Hector, first
struck under my spear, lose his spirit,
sentences.i: unless Hector is first struck by my spear and loses his life,
sentences.n: αἴ κε μή is ‘unless’, with the subjunctive ὀλέσσῃ. πρῶτος is ‘first’, before Achilles dies. ὑπὸ δουρί is ‘under the spear’, and τυπείς is the aorist passive participle of τύπτω ‘struck’. ἀπὸ θυμὸν ὀλέσσῃ is ‘loses his spirit’, where θυμός is the life that leaves the body.

sentences.t: Πατρόκλοιο δ’ ἕλωρα Μενοιτιάδεω ἀποτίσῃ.
sentences.l: and pay the price for the prey of Patroclus, Menoetius’ son.”
sentences.i: and pays the price for the prey he made of Patroclus, son of Menoetius.”
sentences.n: ἀποτίσῃ is an aorist subjunctive of ἀποτίνω ‘pay back’. ἕλωρα is the plural of ἕλωρ ‘prey’, ‘prey, booty’; the Greek does not say what is paid for (the killing, the body or the armour), and the English keeps to ‘the prey he made of Patroclus’. Μενοιτιάδεω is the patronymic, ‘son of Menoetius’. The speech ends on the vow of revenge.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε Θέτις κατὰ δάκρυ χέουσα·
sentences.l: Him then in turn addressed Thetis, down a tear shedding:
sentences.i: Then Thetis, shedding tears, spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: A whole-line reply formula with αὖτε, ‘in turn’, as at 11.837. κατὰ δάκρυ χέουσα, ‘shedding tears’, is the phrase used of Thetis herself at 1.413. The line begins a new paragraph.

sentences.t:
ὠκύμορος δή μοι τέκος ἔσσεαι, οἷ’ ἀγορεύεις·
αὐτίκα γάρ τοι ἔπειτα μεθ’ Ἕκτορα πότμος ἑτοῖμος.
sentences.l:
“Swift-doomed indeed you will be, my child, by what you say;
for at once, after Hector, your doom is ready.”
sentences.i: “My child, you will be swift to your doom, going by what you say; for straight after Hector your doom stands ready.”
sentences.n: ὠκύμορος is ‘swift-doomed’, ‘swift to your doom’, the word she used of him at 1.417. οἷ’ ἀγορεύεις is ‘such things as you say’, meaning ‘from what you say’. αὐτίκα … μεθ’ Ἕκτορα is ‘at once after Hector’. πότμος is ‘doom’, and ἑτοῖμος ‘ready’: Achilles’ vow to kill Hector has just set the order.
